To determine whether the proposed solution's final answer is correct, we can test the claim that $d(n,q) = q^n$.

### 1. Construction of a Codeword of Weight $2q^{n-1}$
Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be two distinct hyperplanes in $\mathrm{PG}(n,q)$. Define the vector $c \in \mathbb{F}_p^{\#\text{points}}$ by:
$$
c(P) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } P \in H_1 \setminus H_2, \\
-1 & \text{if } P \in H_2 \setminus H_1, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Let $\ell$ be any line in $\mathrm{PG}(n,q)$:
- If $\ell \subseteq H_1 \cap H_2$, then $c(P) = 0$ for all $P \in \ell$, so $\sum_{P \in \ell} c(P) = 0$.
- If $\ell \subseteq H_1$ and $\ell \not\subseteq H_2$, then $\ell$ intersects $H_2$ in exactly $1$ point (where $c = 0$), and the remaining $q$ points lie in $H_1 \setminus H_2$ (where $c = 1$). The sum along $\ell$ is $q \cdot 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
- If $\ell \subseteq H_2$ and $\ell \not\subseteq H_1$, by symmetry the sum along $\ell$ is $-q \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
- If $\ell \not\subseteq H_1$ and $\ell \not\subseteq H_2$, $\ell$ intersects $H_1$ in at most one point $P_1$ and $H_2$ in at most one point $P_2$:
  - If $P_1 = P_2 \in H_1 \cap H_2$, then $c(P) = 0$ for all $P \in \ell$.
  - If $P_1 \neq P_2$, then $c(P_1) = 1$, $c(P_2) = -1$, and $c(P) = 0$ for all other points on $\ell$, giving a sum of $1 + (-1) = 0$.

In all cases, $\sum_{P \in \ell} c(P) = 0 \pmod p$, so $c \in \mathcal{C}_1(n,q)^\perp$.

### 2. Weight of the Construction
The size of $H_1 \setminus H_2$ is:
$$
|H_1 \setminus H_2| = \frac{q^n - 1}{q - 1} - \frac{q^{n-1} - 1}{q - 1} = q^{n-1}.
$$
Similarly, $|H_2 \setminus H_1| = q^{n-1}$. Therefore:
$$
\mathrm{wt}(c) = 2q^{n-1}.
$$

For any $q > 2$, we have $2q^{n-1} < q^n$. Hence, $d(n,q) \le 2q^{n-1} < q^n$, which directly contradicts the proposed solution's answer of $q^n$. (The actual general relation is $d(n,q) = q^{n-2} d(2,q)$).

VERDICT: REJECT
